frames.narration: An engineer on the checkout team wants to raise the rollout of the flag new-checkout from 10% to 30%. She submits a change request in the console. In production, the workflow holds it until the owning team approves.
A teammate reviews it and approves. The workflow records who asked, who approved, when, the reason, and the old and new values in the audit log, so the change can be traced and undone later.

messages.label: who, what, when, before and after

frames.narration: The workflow applies the change. The flag service stores it, produces a new numbered ruleset, version 42, with new-checkout at 3,000 out of 10,000, and publishes the file to the CDN.

The service tells the stream gateway, which pushes a short message to the 20,000 connected SDKs. Each one fetches version 42 from the CDN. Instances that rely on polling pick it up at their next poll, within the poll interval plus the cache lifetime.
Later a request from user-123 reaches the checkout service. The code asks the SDK whether new-checkout is on for this user. This is a call inside the process, with no network.

The SDK checks the kill switch (off), then the targeting rules (no match), then hashes the salt and the user id. The result is bucket 2,718. Since 2,718 is below the rollout of 3,000, the flag is on. At 10% the limit was 1,000, so she was off before. Anyone whose bucket was below 1,000 is still on, so no one lost the feature.

Because new-checkout is part of an experiment, the SDK queues an exposure event with the user, the flag, the variation and the ruleset version. Repeats for the same user are dropped, and events leave in batches of a few hundred, so the check itself stays fast.

Over the next days the analysis joins exposures with purchases and compares the 30% who see the new checkout with the 70% who do not. It first checks that the split is really about 30 to 70, and then shows the difference in conversion with a confidence interval, which tells the team whether to go to 100%.
